rationale: B wins because it walks straight into the hard story instead of treating it as a side hazard: "Toast wants to be its restaurants' bank. It won't say how many of them default." A has good bones, but it blinks by refusing "Toast responds to fee criticism" while still trying to sell "Restaurants are borrowing from their point-of-sale system instead of their bank." A also lets "Toast got profitable by selling money, not hardware" overstate the supplied facts; B mostly turns those same gaps into proof demands before anyone emails a reporter.
gaps_in_A: "Toast got profitable by selling money, not hardware" overclaims causality. The update says Toast recently reached profitability and says fintech is higher-margin than hardware; it does not say lending caused profitability.
"underwritten by the payment flow Toast already sees" is not in the fact block. That belongs in "proof it needs," not in the pitchable premise.
"Toast responds to fee criticism" as `no_why_now_but_required` is too timid. Bundling lending is the why-now that makes fee complaints and undisclosed defaults relevant.

The finance angles are strong but crowded: "The cash register wants to be the bank" and "Restaurants are borrowing from their point-of-sale system instead of their bank" lean on the same embedded-finance spine more than A admits.
gaps_in_B: "Toast's path to profit runs through lending, not point-of-sale hardware" still overstates the record. Higher margin does not prove lending is the path to profitability.
"turning point-of-sale into the operating account" pushes beyond the update. No operating account, bank account, or underwriting mechanic was supplied.
"high turnover" in the payroll angle is plausible industry context, but it is imported. Source it or move it into the proof list.
"This story will likely get written whether or not Toast pitches it" is a useful warning, but it is a strategic hunch dressed as inevitability.
